title: The pilgrim's beginning
hookLine: the Way of a Pilgrim: he hears pray without ceasing and sets off to learn how
tomorrow: what would a prayer sound like if it kept time with your heart?

cards: Phones ping all day: drink water, stand up, breathe. One line from Paul can't be set as a reminder at all: “Pray without ceasing.”
A man in a Russian book, The Way of a Pilgrim, hears it read in church, and this time it stops him. People have to eat, work, sleep. How can anyone pray without ceasing?
So he sets off with a knapsack, some dry bread and a Bible, to find out. Christians have answered his question in two different ways.

teach.b: He asks preachers and learned people. They praise prayer, warmly. Nobody tells him how to do what Paul actually said.
Here are the two answers his question runs between. The first is old.

teach.h: ONE: A WHOLE LIFE AS PRAYER.
teach.b: Origen, an early Christian teacher, wrote in his book On Prayer that whoever joins prayer to the deeds that are due, and right deeds to prayer, is praying without ceasing. The whole life becomes one great prayer.
Meals, work, kindness, all of it counts. Its case: Paul can't mean words every second, so he must mean a life turned toward God. The second is the answer the pilgrim finally gets.
An elder, a monk, listens to him and doesn't brush him off.
Unceasing prayer, the elder says, is the Jesus Prayer: a short line said again and again, inwardly, from the heart. Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.
And he puts in the pilgrim's hands the Philokalia, an old collection of writings on prayer. Its case: a life only becomes prayer if something in it keeps praying.
Both readings claim the same verse, and each has kept its own followers.

teach.h: HE WON'T SKIP THE HARD WORD.
teach.b: What makes the pilgrim worth reading is that he won't take a fine answer that skips the hard word.
Without ceasing. He wants the how, and he walks until he gets it.

how: Some Orthodox Christians learn the Jesus Prayer from an elder or spiritual guide, as the pilgrim did, and some pray it with a prayer rope; other Christians speak of offering work and meals as part of a life of prayer.

games.q: who answered what — tap the pairs.
p: a whole life as one great prayer
the Jesus Prayer, again and again

s: the pilgrim gets his answer from the first sermon he hears
preachers praise prayer, but no one tells him how until he meets the elder.
pray without ceasing means you must never do anything else
neither reading says that: one joins prayer to deeds, the other keeps a short prayer going inside them.
the elder gives him the Philokalia, a collection on prayer
and teaches him the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.

games.q: you like the elder's answer: a short prayer kept going all day. state the other reading, Origen's, at its strongest.
o: prayer joined to right deeds makes the whole life one prayer, so no hour is left out.
words don't matter to God at all; only good deeds count.
praying all the time is impossible, so Paul didn't really mean it.
games.why: Origen's best case: Paul's line covers the whole of life, deeds included. the elder answers that something must keep praying inside it. both claim the same verse.

practice: Choose one person whose way of praying, or of staying steady, you've wondered about: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor. Write them a short message that asks it plainly, how do you pray? or what keeps you steady?
Send it now or save it; for the rest of the sit, hold the question open, the way the pilgrim did.

wordCard.voice: The pilgrim's beginning. One line that won't let go, two old answers, and a man who walks until someone shows him how.

orig.note: Paul's Greek for 'without ceasing' in 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

carryVoice: Carry this: how to pray always? He walked a long way rather than drop the hard word. That's sixteen sixty-nine.
